_comment: Neurofebric kernel policy. Ported from the legacy harness policies/default_policy.yaml;
see docs/POLICY_PORT.md for the concept-by-concept mapping and the four places the
two do not line up. Rules are evaluated in this order and any denial stops evaluation:
deniedTools -> allowedTools -> limits -> command patterns -> secret-write patterns ->
paths -> write size. These rules can only ever REMOVE a permission. Approval and denial
of the tool's risk tier is decided by platform/core/policy.ts, which runs afterwards.
_allowedToolsNote: An empty list means no name-based gating, NOT 'everything is allowed'. Every tool is
still classified by its risk tier and must clear policy.ts. Name a tool in both lists
_fileRulesNote: Ordered, first match wins, and the catch-all above means: anything inside the roots
from .pi/neurofebric.json is fair game. A path that is outside every root, escapes via
.., or resolves outside through a symlink or junction is denied by the boundary before
these rules are consulted, so '**' can only ever mean 'inside the root'.
To lock a subtree down, insert e.g. { "pattern": ".env*", "read": "deny", "write": "deny" }
_destructiveCommandPatternsNote: Case-insensitive substrings matched against COMMAND text only (the command, cmd, script,
shell, shellCommand, args or argv arguments; for a shell tool the whole payload). They
apply at every tool tier, because these name operations that destroy state rather than
content that merely looks alarming. Quoting one inside a document is not an operation, so
file content is deliberately not scanned.
_destructiveCommandTokensNote: THE DELETION GUARD, and the reason it exists: bash is a permitted tool and the Pi
integration has no separate denied delete tool, so a deletion issued through the shell is
reachable no matter which tool names it. These are the only place it can be stopped, so
they are matched as WHOLE TOKENS in command text at every tool tier.
Token matching (not substring) is what makes the rule explicit instead of an accidental
over-match: 'rm', 'rm -f', 'rm -rf', 'rm -r -f', 'rm -fr' and plain 'rm file' are all the
same decision, and a word that merely contains 'rm' is NOT caught. This is why 'rm -rf' is
not relied on as the sole deletion rule.
SCOPE BOUNDARY: command text only. A write whose payload merely contains the string
'rm -rf' is ALLOWED, because documenting a command is not running it. Injected content is
still caught, because it arrives inside command text: 'bash -c "rm -rf /"' is denied.
This is a guardrail, not a sandbox. It cannot constrain what an already-permitted command
does, and it is not a substitute for OS-level isolation, which remains deferred.
_secretWritePatternsNote: Case-insensitive substrings matched ONLY against the content payload of a write-tier
is the point: a secret must not be PERSISTED, while reading or searching for one is
ordinary analysis. These are deliberately NOT applied to read or search arguments, so
a grep for 'password' is allowed. The path argument is not scanned either: a file named
secret is scoped to secret: so vault prose may be authored; a JSON-quoted secret key that slips this gate is still caught by the redaction plane at persistence.
